Artisanal describes something made by a skilled person using their hands, craft knowledge, and careful attention — rather than being churned out by machines in a factory.

When you call something artisanal, you are saying three things at once: who made it (a skilled individual), how it was made (by hand, with care and expertise), and how much was made (in small amounts, not thousands at a time).

Think of the difference between a loaf of bread baked by a skilled baker who watches the dough, adjusts for the weather, shapes it by hand, and knows exactly when it's ready — versus a loaf that rolled off a conveyor belt in a factory alongside 10,000 identical loaves that morning. The first loaf is artisanal. The second is not.

The word almost always carries these qualities together:

  • Made by hand — human hands do the significant work, not machines.
  • Made with skill — the person making it has learned their craft and is good at it. It's not just "homemade" by anyone; it implies real expertise.
  • Made in small batches — not mass-produced. The maker can give real attention to each item.
  • Made with care for quality — the goal is to make something good, not just to make something fast or cheap.

This is the detail most people miss. "Artisanal" is not simply a fancy word for "handmade." Your neighbour making jam for the first time using a recipe they found online is handmade — but it isn't really artisanal. Artisanal implies that the maker has mastered their craft. They have deep knowledge, years of practice, and a trained eye (or hand, or palate). The result shows it.

Think of a watchmaker who assembles each timepiece by hand with precision tools and decades of experience. Or a cheesemaker who knows how temperature, aging time, and bacterial cultures interact to create a specific flavour. That level of knowledge and care is the heart of what "artisanal" means.

The word only fully makes sense when you understand what it's not:

  • Mass production — factories making thousands of identical products using machines, with speed and low cost as the main goals. There is no individual skill or personal attention involved.
  • Industrial — large-scale, standardised, built for efficiency rather than quality or craft.

Artisanal sits at the opposite end of this spectrum. Scale is small. Attention is high. The maker's individual skill visibly shapes the outcome.

The word is used across many areas of life:

  • Food and drink — artisanal bread, cheese, coffee, chocolate, beer, olive oil, pasta. These are made in small batches by skilled producers who care about the quality of ingredients and the process.
  • Furniture and woodwork — a carpenter who designs and builds each piece individually by hand.
  • Clothing and textiles — garments sewn and tailored by skilled hands, not assembled in bulk factories.
  • Jewelry — each piece shaped, soldered, and finished by a craftsperson rather than stamped out by a machine.
  • Pottery and ceramics — each item thrown on a wheel or formed by hand, with natural variation between pieces.
A Subtle but Important Point: Variation Is a Feature

With mass-produced goods, every item looks identical — that's the point. With artisanal goods, small differences between individual items are normal and even valued. A slight variation in the crust of a loaf, a small irregularity in a handmade bowl — these aren't flaws. They are evidence of human hands and individual skill at work. They are proof that something is genuinely artisanal.
The Word in Modern Life — A Word of Caution

In recent years, "artisanal" has become very popular in advertising and marketing. Companies sometimes put the label on products that don't really deserve it — to make mass-produced items sound more special and premium than they are. So while the word has a precise and honest meaning, you will sometimes encounter it being used loosely or misleadingly as a marketing trick.

When used honestly, though, it points to something real and valuable: a product made by a human being who has mastered a craft, put genuine skill into their work, and cared about the outcome.
Artisanal means: made by a skilled craftsperson, by hand, in small quantities, with careful attention to quality — as opposed to being mass-produced by machines.
